verdicts.note: Atlantic (live, 200): "Weaknesses that have plagued Martin's previous books are also present: too much repetition, unexceptional prose, and characters who use the same idioms..." Quote verbatim; every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: cries out for better editing, it remains entirely engrossing
verdicts.note: Atlantic (live): "But while A Dance with Dragons cries out for better editing, it remains entirely engrossing." Quote verbatim; both limbs on page.

verdicts.trueWording: I've always agreed with William Faulkner
verdicts.note: Atlantic (live), Martin's first answer: "I've always agreed with William Faulkner-- he said that the human heart in conflict with itself is the only thing worth writing about." Verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: and the rest is just set dressing
verdicts.note: Atlantic (live): "I've always taken that as my guiding principle, and the rest is just set dressing. I mean, you can have a dragon, you can have a science fiction story set on a distant planet with aliens and starships..." Dragons and settings limb supported by the following sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: bliss to be found in the word-drunk naming of places
verdicts.note: NYT via Wayback raw capture 20251024170837id_ (live URL 403, DataDome): "Still, there's bliss to be found in the word-drunk naming of places -- the Frostfangs, Sea Dragon Point, Rook's Rest -- and people". All three place names present.

verdicts.trueWording: Wick Whittlestick and Pinchface Jon Myre
verdicts.note: NYT (Wayback raw): the same 'bliss' sentence continues "...and people: Homeless Harry Strickland and Bloodbeard, Cotter Pyke and Three-Finger Hobb, Wick Whittlestick and Pinchface Jon Myre." Person-names framed as bliss/pleasure.

verdicts.trueWording: a blunt and bawdy earthiness that befits the son of a Bayonne, N.J., longshoreman
verdicts.note: NYT (Wayback raw), para 2: "Mr. Martin writes fantasy for grown-ups, with a blunt and bawdy earthiness that befits the son of a Bayonne, N.J., longshoreman." Verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: a sprawling and panoramic 19th-century novel turned out in fantasy motley
verdicts.note: NYT (Wayback raw), para 2: "The series... is like a sprawling and panoramic 19th-century novel turned out in fantasy motley, more Balzac and Dickens than Tolkien." Both limbs verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: In a work this size... a summary up front would be useful
verdicts.note: NYT (Wayback raw): "In a work this size it's the reader who must embark on a harrowing quest, and a summary up front would be useful." 'to the reader' is the same sentence's subject.

verdicts.trueWording: a mammoth novel that so far totals 1,742,848 words
verdicts.note: NYT (Wayback raw): "it's just a 1,016-page installment in a mammoth novel that so far totals 1,742,848 words." The 'mammoth novel' is the cycle; figure exact.

verdicts.trueWording: Jennings's own phrase, not attributed to Martin
verdicts.note: NYT (Wayback raw): "He's often more intrigued by the friction among conflicting religions, by the Kremlinology of Westeros, in the 'plots, ploys, whispers, lies, secrets within secrets' that make of up 'the game of thrones.'" Quote verbatim and the 'more intrigued... than fantasy's usual furniture' contrast is carried by the preceding sentence ('The elements of fantasy exist here but are deftly muted'), but the page nowhere has Martin calling it that -- the coinage is the reviewer's.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the claim's 'what he calls' -- attributing the phrase 'the Kremlinology of Westeros' to Martin; on the page it is Jennings's own wording, with no attribution to Martin

verdicts.trueWording: The elements of fantasy exist here but are deftly muted
verdicts.note: NYT (Wayback raw): "The elements of fantasy exist here but are deftly muted, as Mr. Martin defies genre conventions." Verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: his medieval realms ring with echoes of our own time
verdicts.note: NYT (Wayback raw): "All the while his medieval realms ring with echoes of our own time, of our modern terrorscapes that rage with liars, spies and true believers." Verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: Mr. Martin is a literary dervish, enthralled by complicated characters and vivid language
verdicts.note: NYT (Wayback raw): full sentence continues "and bursting with the wild vision of the very best tale tellers." Verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: bizarre and beautifully imaginative set-pieces on haunted rivers and in the supernatural North
verdicts.note: Locus (live, 200), byline 'by Jeff VanderMeer', headed 'A Dozen of the Best from 2011', dated February 5, 2012: "a huge, dense novel that devotes several scenes to bizarre and beautifully imaginative set-pieces on haunted rivers and in the supernatural North." Author, title, date and quote all confirmed.
